hook: A SQL engine with **no server, no install drama** — that queries your files directly. This one earns its keep daily.
chapters: DuckDB vs SQLite vs SQL Server

scenes.title: Analytics SQL, **embedded** — like SQLite for analytics
scenes.sub: In-process, columnar, and ruthless about skipping work

lines: # pandas too small? no server to be had?

scenes.narration: DuckDB is an analytics database that runs inside your process — no server, no service, pip install duckdb and you're querying. Think SQLite's embedding model, but built for analytics: columnar storage, vectorized execution, and a query optimizer that prunes columns and partitions before reading. It lives naturally in notebooks, scripts, and data pipelines — wherever you'd reach for pandas but your data got too big, or you'd reach for a database but there's no server to be had.

do: no daemon · no credentials · no container

scenes.narration: Why it lands so well. Installation is one package — no daemon, no credentials file, no container. SQL is the Postgres dialect you mostly know — CTEs, window functions, all of it. And the engine is modern: columnar vectors, multi-threading, late materialization — the tricks big warehouses use, minus the warehouse. For a .NET architect, the right mental model is: an embedded OLAP engine. SQLite taught the world embedded OLTP; DuckDB is the same idea for analytics.

scenes.title: SELECT * FROM **'file.parquet'** — yes, literally
scenes.sub: CSV, JSON, Parquet — files are tables

lines: -- no load · no import · no staging

scenes.narration: Here's the party trick that changes your workflow: DuckDB queries files directly, by path, in SQL. Select star from quote events dot csv quote — the file is the table. Parquet especially shines: only the columns you name get read, and partitioned folder trees are pruned automatically — last chapter's work pays off here. No load step, no import, no staging table. Your data lake becomes queryable the moment the files land.

steps.at: Any file path in a FROM clause

do: one logical table, matching files only

scenes.narration: The mechanics. Any file path in a FROM clause — CSV, Parquet, JSON. Glob patterns work, so partitioned lakes are queried as one logical table while the engine opens only matching files. Inference is good but verify with describe when it matters — CSV types are guesses, and last chapter taught you what guesses are worth. For production pipelines, the read dot functions with explicit options replace inference with specification. Files in, answers out, nothing in between.

scenes.title: Join **CSV to Parquet to DataFrame** — why not?

lines: JOIN refs.json r ON r.k = f.k
JOIN my_df m ON m.id = f.id

do: CSV + Parquet + JSON in one SQL
a pandas DataFrame joins the files

steps.at: collapses what used to be an ETL project

scenes.narration: Because files are tables, joins span formats without ceremony: your dimension list as CSV, your facts as partitioned Parquet, your reference data as a JSON file — one SQL joins them all. Even better, DuckDB speaks Arrow natively, so an in-memory pandas DataFrame registers as a table and joins the files. This collapses what used to be an ETL project into a query. The integration pattern of the modern data stack is smaller than you were taught.

do: SQL sees your live pandas object

scenes.narration: Three integration moves. Cross-file joins with plain SQL — formats stop mattering. Register a DataFrame as a virtual table and SQL sees your live pandas object — perfect for the notebook workflow where some data was computed in Python. And results return in whatever shape you need — dataframe, Arrow table, or plain rows. When your agent needs to answer a question over files, this is the query layer — no database to provision, no data to move.

scenes.title: duckdb.sql() — SQL as a **Python expression**

do: lazy until you ask for results

scenes.narration: The Python API is refreshingly small. DuckDB dot sql runs a query and returns a relation — lazy, chainable, printable. Dot df converts to a DataFrame; dot arrow to Arrow; dot fetchall to rows. Parameters are bound, not concatenated — the injection rules from Reel 7 apply to SQL strings as they do anywhere. And relations chain: filter then aggregate then to dataframe, each step still lazy until you ask for results. That's the whole API — an hour to learn, a career to exploit.

The idioms. Parameterize from day one — question marks and params, never f-string SQL. Chain lazy relations when building pipelines — the optimizer fuses steps you'd otherwise materialize. And explore the extensions: httpfs queries files over S3 or HTTP as if local; spatial adds geometry; full-text search is built in. DuckDB's answer to 'can it do X' is usually 'install the extension' — that extensibility is why it's become the Swiss army engine of the data world.

The comparison everyone asks about. SQLite: row-oriented, battle-tested for transactional workloads — your app's local database. DuckDB: column-oriented, built for scans and aggregations — your analysis engine. Different shapes of embedded. And SQL Server? That's the enterprise system of record — concurrent transactional workloads, permissions, HA. You don't replace it; you EXPORT from it to Parquet and analyze with DuckDB. Each engine owns its workload.

do: point it at last night’s export

scenes.narration: Where each lives in your architecture. SQL Server keeps serving the application — you know this world deeply. DuckDB sits beside it for everything analytical: point it at last night's export and ask questions. And note the agent angle — when you build the text-to-SQL agent in later stages, DuckDB means the demo needs zero infrastructure: files plus an in-process engine. That's the kind of dependency decision that makes prototypes demo-able in a day.

scenes.title: Results in, results out — **files again**
scenes.sub: CREATE TABLE … AS, COPY TO Parquet, in-memory persistence
scenes.narration: Closing the loop: DuckDB persists when you ask it to. In-memory by default — gone when the process ends. For durability: create a database file, or materialize results back to the lake. Copy to writes query results straight to Parquet — including partitioned output. The round trip is elegant: files in, SQL in the middle, files out. No import jobs, no staging schemas, no server to babysit. Your pipeline is a query and a copy statement.

The persistence patterns. Default in-memory for exploration — zero cleanup. A connect with a filename when tables must survive — full database semantics, still no server. And copy to for the lake round trip: run the transformation, write partitioned Parquet straight out. Views let you layer logic without materializing each step. This is why DuckDB ends so many architecture debates: the same engine explores interactively, runs the nightly pipeline, and serves the agent's ad-hoc questions — all from files.

opts: It stores data in a single file like SQLite
It's embedded/in-process with zero infrastructure, but columnar and optimized for analytical scans
It replaces SQLite in mobile apps
quiz.why: The embedding model (in-process, no server) is SQLite's; the engine is columnar/vectorized for OLAP workloads — the OLTP/OLAP distinction is the point.

quiz.q: How do you query only March data from a year=/month= partitioned Parquet lake in DuckDB?
opts: Load all files into pandas first
Write WHERE month = '03' — the engine prunes partitions and files automatically
quiz.why: Hive-style partitioning + Parquet metadata let DuckDB skip files that can't match — pruning happens before any data is read.

quiz.q: When would you choose SQLite over DuckDB?
opts: For transactional app storage — many small concurrent reads/writes with ACID guarantees
quiz.why: Row-store + transaction engine = OLTP workloads (apps). DuckDB's columnar engine shines at scans/aggregations, not concurrent row updates.

code.title: DuckDB — the daily workflow in one script
code.body:
import duckdb

# --- explore files directly -------------------------------------
rel = duckdb.sql("""
    SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS n, SUM(amount) AS total
    FROM 'data/events.csv'
    GROUP BY status
    ORDER BY total DESC
""")
print(rel)                     # lazy relation — pretty-prints a sample

# --- join CSV to a partitioned Parquet lake ----------------------
duckdb.sql("""
    CREATE VIEW events AS
    SELECT e.*, c.team
    FROM 'data/events.csv' e
    JOIN 'lake/customers/year=*/month=03/*.parquet' c USING (cust_id)
""")

# --- register a live pandas DataFrame ----------------------------
import pandas as pd
flags = pd.DataFrame({"status": ["P1", "P2"], "sla_h": [1, 24]})
duckdb.register("flags", flags)

result = duckdb.sql("""
    SELECT e.team, f.sla_h, AVG(e.amount) AS avg_amt
    FROM events e
    JOIN flags f USING (status)
    GROUP BY ALL
    ORDER BY avg_amt DESC
""").df()

# --- persist the pipeline -----------------------------------------
duckdb.sql("""
    COPY (SELECT * FROM events WHERE status = 'P1')
    TO 'out/p1_cases.parquet' (FORMAT PARQUET, COMPRESSION 'snappy')
""")

# Parameterized (the only safe way to mix variables + SQL):
city = "Paris"
safe = duckdb.sql("SELECT * FROM events WHERE city = ?", params=[city])
annot: duckdb.register — the DataFrame stays live; SQL sees edits instantly
? params — never f-string SQL; same injection discipline as any database

notes:
# DuckDB

## What it is
- Embedded, in-process, columnar OLAP engine. `pip install duckdb` — no server.
- Postgres-flavored SQL; vectorized + parallel; works beyond RAM.

## Query files directly
- `FROM 'data.csv' / 'lake/**/*.parquet'` — files are tables.
- Partitioned folders pruned automatically; globs supported.

## Joins across files
- csv ⨝ parquet ⨝ JSON in one query.
- `duckdb.register('name', df)` — live pandas DataFrame as a SQL view.
- Results: `.df()` / `.arrow()` / `.fetchall()`.

## Python integration
- `duckdb.sql("...", params=[...])` — lazy relation, chainable.
- Extensions: `httpfs` (S3/HTTP), spatial, FTS.

## DuckDB vs SQLite vs SQL Server
| Engine | Job |
| --- | --- |
| SQLite | embedded OLTP (app storage, transactions) |
| DuckDB | embedded OLAP (analytics over files) |
| SQL Server | enterprise system of record |

## Persisting & exporting
- In-memory by default; `duckdb.connect('file.db')` persists.
- `COPY (SELECT …) TO 'out.parquet' (FORMAT PARQUET, PARTITION_BY (col))`.
- Compose with views; materialize only what's expensive.
